papers.full_text_excerpt:
[Abstract] Large Language Models (LLMs) showcase impressive capabilities but encounter challenges like hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent, untraceable reasoning processes. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating knowledge from external databases. This enhances the accuracy and credibility of the generation, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks, and allows for continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information. RAG synergistically merges LLMs’ intrinsic knowledge with the vast, dynamic repositories of external databases. This comprehensive review paper offers a detailed examination of the progression of RAG paradigms, encompassing the Naive RAG, the Advanced RAG, and the Modular RAG. It meticulously scrutinizes the tripartite foundation of RAG frameworks, which includes the retrieval, the generation and the augmentation techniques. The paper highlights the state-of-the-art technologies embedded in each of these critical components, providing a profound understanding of the advancements in RAG systems. Furthermore, this paper introduces up-to-date evaluation framework and benchmark. At the end, this article delineates the challenges currently faced and points out prospective avenues for research and development 111Resources are available at https://github.com/Tongji-KGLLM/RAG-Survey .

[I Introduction] Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success, though they still face significant limitations, especially in domain-specific or knowledge-intensive tasks [1], notably producing “hallucinations” [2] when handling queries beyond their training data or requiring current information. To overcome challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by retrieving relevant document chunks from external knowledge base through semantic similarity calculation. By referencing external knowledge, RAG effectively reduces the problem of generating factually incorrect content. Its integration into LLMs has resulted in widespread adoption, establishing RAG as a key technology in advancing chatbots and enhancing the suitability of LLMs for real-world applications.

RAG technology has rapidly developed in recent years, and the technology tree summarizing related research is shown in Figure 1. The development trajectory of RAG in the era of large models exhibits several distinct stage characteristics. Initially, RAG’s inception coincided with the rise of the Transformer architecture, focusing on enhancing language models by incorporating additional knowledge through Pre-Training Models (PTM). This early stage was characterized by foundational work aimed at refining pre-training techniques[3, 4, 5].The subsequent arrival of ChatGPT [6] marked a pivotal moment, with LLM demonstrating powerful in context learning (ICL) capabilities. RAG research shifted towards providing

[IV-A2 Context Selection/Compression] s and SLMs. In this paradigm, SLMs serve as filters, while LLMs function as reordering agents. The research shows that instructing LLMs to rearrange challenging samples identified by SLMs leads to significant improvements in various Information Extraction (IE) tasks. Another straightforward and effective approach involves having the LLM evaluate the retrieved content before generating the final answer. This allows the LLM to filter out documents with poor relevance through LLM critique. For instance, in Chatlaw [104], the LLM is prompted to self-suggestion on the referenced legal provisions to assess their relevance.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLM) have made automatic code generation possible for real-world programming tasks in general-purpose programming languages such as Python. papers.abstract: Integrating large language models (LLMs) into healthcare can enhance workflow efficiency and patient care by automating tasks such as summarising consultations. papers.abstract: Abstract Information Extraction (IE) aims to extract structural knowledge from plain natural language texts. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances in generic question-answering (QA) but often suffer from domain gaps and outdated knowledge in smart manufacturing (SM). papers.title: Operational AI Deployment Assurance: Governance-State Orchestration Under Threshold-Sensitive Deployment Conditions -- A Governance Framework for High-Stakes AI Systems
papers.abstract: AI governance frameworks increasingly emphasize fairness, transparency, accountability, and lifecycle risk management in high-stakes domains. However, many current approaches remain observational, relying on static metric reporting, post-hoc auditing, and monitoring dashboards without directly governing deployment readiness, remediation progression, escalation states, or assurance-driven deployment control. papers.title: Expert Mind: A Retrieval-Augmented Architecture for Expert Knowledge Preservation in the Energy Sector
papers.abstract: The departure of subject-matter experts from industrial organizations results in the irreversible loss of tacit knowledge that is rarely captured through conventional documentation practices. This paper proposes Expert Mind, an experimental system that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), large language models (LLMs), and multimodal capture techniques to preserve, structure, and make queryable the deep expertise of organizational knowledge holders. Drawing on the specific context of the energy sector, where decades of operational experience risk being lost to an aging workforce, we ...[truncated]

papers.title: EHR-RAGp: Retrieval-Augmented Prototype-Guided Foundation Model for Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHR) contain rich longitudinal patient information and are widely used in predictive modeling applications. However, effectively leveraging historical data remains challenging due to long trajectories, heterogeneous events, temporal irregularity, and the varying relevance of past clinical context. Existing approaches often rely on fixed windows or uniform aggregation, which can obscure clinically important signals. papers.title: RecoAtlas: From Semantic Plausibility to Set-Level Utility in LLM Recommendation Agents
papers.abstract: LLM recommendation agents increasingly produce structured recommendation reports: sets of items accompanied by natural-language justifications. Yet existing evaluations often reduce this setting to reranking small shortlisted candidate sets or judge reports mainly by semantic plausibility. We introduce Recommendation Atlas (Agentic Tool-Level Assessment for Shopping), or RecoAtlas, a benchmark and toolkit for evaluating shopping agents with behavior-grounded metrics. report_markdown: ## Overview Tool use and function calling enable large language model (LLM) agents to transcend static knowledge by interacting with external APIs, databases, and domain-specific software. While these capabilities unlock powerful automation for scientific discovery, enterprise analytics, and recommendation systems, they also surface critical gaps around integration robustness, security, determinism, and evaluation. ## Landscape Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a primary approach for granting LLMs access to external knowledge, mitigating hallucinations and outdated internal knowledge [17, 19]. In specialized domains, tool-augmented agents such as ChemCrow integrate 18 chemistry tools to plan syntheses and predict properties [18, 31], while GeneGPT teaches LLMs to use NCBI Web APIs for genomics question answering [29]. Beyond retrieval, agentic architectures structure LLM behavior around tool calls, prompt engineering, and reasoning loops [30, 14], and enterprise-oriented systems increasingly enforce contracts, auditability, and deterministic outputs through harness engineering [46] or governed analytics APIs [43]. At the same time, the blurred boundary between data and instructions in LLM-integrated applications exposes them to indirect prompt injection attacks [23]. Evaluation efforts remain nascent, with recent benchmarks like RecoAtlas [50] proposing behavior-grounded metrics for structured recommendation outputs, and agent evaluation surveys [39] highlighting the need for enterprise-scale assessment. ## Research gaps - **LLMs lack built-in mechanisms to access and utilize external tools and knowledge sources, limiting their effectiveness in specialized domains such as chemistry and genomics.** (confidence: high) LLMs intrinsically struggle with hallucination, outdated knowledge, and opaque reasoning [17]. Current solutions retrofit domain-specific tools through prompting and APIs [18, 29] but do not provide a native, general-purpose mechanism for external tool use [14, 30]. - **LLM-integrated applications are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks because the boundary between data and instructions is blurred, creating new security risks for tool-using agents.** (confidence: high) Prompts embedded in data that an LLM later processes can manipulate the agent’s behavior remotely, as demonstrated by attacks on real-world LLM-integrated apps [23]. This directly impacts the safety of agents that call tools based on external content. - **LLMs continue to suffer from hallucinations and reliance on outdated internal knowledge, which retrieval-augmented tools aim to address, but robust integration remains an open challenge.** (confidence: high) RAG systems provide external knowledge to improve accuracy [17, 19]. However, domain-specific tool integration (e.g., in chemistry [18]) remains brittle, and there is no universal standard for seamlessly merging retrieved facts with LLM generation without introducing inconsistency or latency [35, 48]. - **RAG systems lack robust mechanisms for LLMs to autonomously validate or critique the relevance of retrieved documents before generation, relying on naive semantic similarity without deeper contextual verification.** (confidence: high) While one straightforward improvement is to have the LLM itself evaluate and filter retrieved content, this approach is still an add-on rather than a built-in capability [17]. Most RAG pipelines use shallow similarity scoring, leaving retrieval quality unverified in context. - **The inherent stochasticity of LLMs prevents their reliable use in high-stakes enterprise environments where deterministic and auditable function calling is required.** (confidence: high) Standard LLM outputs are non‑deterministic, which conflicts with regulatory demands for reproducibility and audit trails. Recent work proposes architectural standards to convert probabilistic intent into deterministic software artifacts [12] and harness‑engineering practices that enforce traceable, auditable agent behavior [46]. The gap remains that these solutions are not yet standardised or widely adopted. - **Current LLM agent evaluation frameworks lack standardized, behavior-grounded metrics for assessing structured, multi-item recommendation outputs beyond semantic plausibility or small candidate re-ranking.** (confidence: medium) Existing evaluations often reduce recommendation tasks to reranking small candidate sets [34] or judge outputs by surface plausibility. RecoAtlas [50] introduces set-level utility metrics like relevance, complementarity, and diversity to fill this metric gap, but such behavior‑grounded benchmarks are not yet mainstream. ## References [1] [R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing (2000)](https://doi.org/10.32614/r.manuals) — R Core Team [2] [Fitting Linear Mixed-Effects Models Using lme4 (2015)](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v067.i01) — Douglas M.
